question.text: This northern neighbor of Germany lies on the Jutland peninsula. It also controls Greenland.
question.clue: This country lost a personal union with a nearby country in the 1814 Treaty of Kiel.

swap.leadin: These people ruled England from 1016 to 1035 under Canute.
swap.text: Name these Norse explorers and warriors who did not actually wear horned helmets.
swap.clue: A tax called these people's geld was paid following their victory at the Battle of Maldon.

question.leadin: The Treaty of Nystad ended this war in 1721, 12 years after a decisive victory over Charles XII at Poltava ended Sweden's time as a European power.
question.text: Name this war motivated by one European power's desire for a port city on the Baltic Sea.
question.clue: During this war, one side relieved a siege during a snowstorm at the Battle of Narva.

swap.leadin: A sniper from this country, Simo Hayha, gained the nickname "White Death" for killing hundreds of Soviet troops without using a scope during the Winter War.
swap.text: Name this country whose fallen soldiers are often buried in the Hietaniemi Cemetery in Helsinki.
swap.answerHtml: Finland [or Republic of Findland or Suomen tasavalta or Republiken Finland or Suomi]
swap.clue: Activists from this country's largest Germanic minority group cited scientific racists to argue that its majority ethnicity was of inferior Mongoloid stock.

question.leadin: The author of the Prose Edda, Snorri Sturluson, was a law speaker of a parliament in this country.
question.text: Name this country home to the Althing, the oldest European parliament that is still functioning.
question.clue: The ruling chiefs of this country established the Althing in the early 900s, one of the oldest continuously meeting parliaments in the world.

swap.text: During the 1600s, Sweden was led by this philosophically-minded queen, the daughter of Gustavus Adolphus. Peter Minuit established a fort named for her in the New World.
swap.clue: Although historians are not sure whether the abdication was influenced by a clandestine love for Cardinal Decio Azzolino, we do know that this ruler received educateion from Jorge Stiernhelm.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about trials of Nazis after World War II.
question.text: Following the war, the death penalty was reinstated in Norway specifically to serve as punishment for this Nazi collaborator, Norway's puppet leader during its occupation.
question.clue: This politician launched their political career in a series of articles explaining their 'political thoughts' on the death of mentor Fritjohf Nansen.

swap.leadin: This country saw a civil war that pitted the White Guard against the Red Guard.
swap.text: Name this northern European country once home to the radical Lapua Movement. It hosted the 1952 Olympics in its capital of Helsinki.
swap.clue: Due to the nationalistic drivings of Johan Snellman, this country underwent a namesake language strife in the 1800s. This country won the Battle of Raate Road.

question.leadin: More soldiers drowned in the rough seas on the way back from a campaign against this city than in capturing a fleet in this city.
question.text: Name this capital city that was bombarded by the British in 1807. A monarch from the House of Oldenburg was crowned in this city's cathedral in 1449.
question.clue: Horatio Nelson allegedly "put the telescope to a blind eye" during a battle for this city.

swap.leadin: Identify these victims of brazen assassinations from European history.
swap.text: South Africa's most evil export, superspy Craig Williamson, may have been responsible for the 1986 shooting of this Swedish Prime Minister, an ardent opponent of Apartheid.
swap.clue: This man claimed that apartheid "cannot be reformed, it has to be eliminated", which Eugene de Kock later testified may have led to his death.

question.leadin: Answer the following about a northern European "Brave Little Democracy's" effort against Soviet Aggression in World War II.
question.text: The Soviets' poor performance during the first stages of the Winter War was largely caused by this array of fortifications named after the Finnish commander-in-chief.
question.clue: Reinforced concrete and protection plates were dropped from this due to a rise in the price of steel, and parts of it were simply strategically placed mounds of soil known as "slope cuts."

swap.text: During the Thirty Years' War, Sweden was led by this ruler of the House of Vasa, dubbed the "Lion of the North."
swap.clue: At the Battle of Lech, also known as the "Battle of Rain," he commanded troops over the Count of Tilly.

question.leadin: Journalist Richard Lowenthal ("REE-kard LEOV-en-tall") originated this term to describe Soviet attempts to expand influence in Central Europe.
question.text: Give this term describing the domination of the politics of a small country by a larger neighbor. It originally referred to relations between the Soviet Union and the country it once fought in the Winter War.
question.answerHtml: Finlandization [or suomettuminen; or Finnlandisierung; or Finlandizatsiya; do not prompt or accept "Finland"]
question.clue: This process where a large power gradually acquires cultural and political influence over a smaller one, as the USSR did to a Scandinavian state during the Cold War.

swap.text: Franklin Scott's "A Saint and a Queen" discusses Margaret and this Swedish saint, who created the "Fifteen O's" prayer and a namesake order open to men and women.

question.text: One Swedish leader during the Thirty Years War was this "lion of the north" who won the Battle of Breitenfeld before getting killed at the Battle of Lutzen.
question.answerHtml: Gustavus Adolphus Magnus [accept Gustav II Adolf; prompt on any partial answer]
question.clue: This ruler's army sang "A Mighty Fortress is Our God" during one of his victories in which Count Tilly was fatally wounded.

swap.text: Finnish became an official language of administration during an "Age of" this concept in Sweden. That era named for this concept saw increased parliamentary power after the Great Northern War.
swap.answerHtml: Age of Liberty [accept frihetstiden or frihet; accept vapauden aika or vapautta]
swap.clue: This era follows an era of imperialism called the Stormaktstiden ("STORM-okts-tee-den").

question.leadin: Name some present and former possessions of Norway.
question.text: This archipelago in the Arctic is the site of the Global Seed Vault on its largest island of Spitsbergen, which contains its center of Longyearben.
question.clue: The name of this Norwegian archipelago means "cold shores," and its three inhabited islands are Spitzbergen, Bear Island, and Hopen.

swap.leadin: The Kuli stone, now found in a museum in this city, describes how a lord who ruled from here tried to force subjects to convert to Christianity.
swap.text: Name this city founded in 997 by Olaf Tryggvason, the medieval capital of Norway.
swap.clue: Jon remained loyal to this city's exiled archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson, who led the Norwegian Riksrad ("reeks-ROAD") until its 1537 dissolution with the Reformation. Pilgrims visited Saint Olaf's shrine at this city's cathedral.

question.leadin: The region of "Serkland" was first mentioned in the Gripsholm Runestone, part of a series of twenty-six runestones named for this man.
question.text: Name this man who sailed down the Volga River to lead a disastrous 1042 expedition in the Caspian Sea, which earned him an epithet referencing his distant voyages.

swap.leadin: This document was drafted by early New Zealand settler and prominent Darwinian Evolution critic D. G. Monrad.
swap.text: Name this progressive document adopted in 1849 to replace the King's Law under pressure from both the National Liberals and Friends of the Peasants. A "November" version of this document created in 1863 sparked an invasion by octogenarian Field Marshall "Papa Wrangel."
swap.answerHtml: The Constitution of Denmark [accept First Constitution of Denmark; accept First Danish Constitution; prompt on Constitution or November Constitution by asking “of what country?”]
